general.query: syncope initial evaluation and risk stratification

results.key_finding: Initial evaluation comprises history, physical examination including supine and standing blood pressure, and a 12-lead ECG. High-risk features (syncope during exertion or supine, palpitations before the event, known structural or coronary disease, family history of sudden death under 40, high-risk ECG findings) call for early in-hospital evaluation with immediate ECG monitoring. Echocardiography is indicated when structural heart disease is known or suspected; EEG, brain imaging and routine laboratory panels are not recommended without a specific indication.
results.title: 2018 ESC Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of syncope (Brignole M et al., Eur Heart J 2018;39:1883-1948)

results.key_finding: Risk stratification at the initial evaluation separates patients needing in-hospital monitoring and cardiac testing from those suitable for outpatient evaluation; targeted rather than routine blood testing is advised.
results.title: 2017 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline for the evaluation and management of patients with syncope (Shen WK et al.)

general.summary: Guidelines base syncope work-up on the initial evaluation (history, examination, orthostatic BP, 12-lead ECG) and risk stratification; high-risk patients receive in-hospital ECG monitoring and targeted cardiac testing.

clinical_pearls: Brief myoclonic jerks are common during syncope (convulsive syncope) and are often misdiagnosed as epilepsy, leading to inappropriate antiseizure treatment
Trifascicular pattern (bifascicular block with first-degree AV block) with syncope calls for inpatient monitoring; documented high-grade AV block is a Class I pacing indication
The ECG in cardiac syncope may not capture the culprit arrhythmia at the time of presentation; the resting ECG findings of conduction disease provide critical diagnostic clues
Thiazide diuretics can cause electrolyte abnormalities (hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia) that exacerbate cardiac conduction abnormalities
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Four required actions (ECG, electrolytes, TTE, telemetry) plus a head CT for the head strike; three red herrings (convulsive jerks, prior orthostatic attribution, mild aortic stenosis).

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Marcus Williams is a 71-year-old man with a history of hypertension on multiple medications, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, and obstructive sleep apnea who presents to the emergency department after a third episode of sudden loss of consciousness in six weeks. Today's episode occurred while he was sitting in a chair watching television at approximately 2:30 PM. His wife, who was in the room, reports that he suddenly became unresponsive and slumped to the left, falling out of the chair onto the floor. She observed brief jerking movements of both arms and legs lasting approximately 10 to 15 seconds. She describes his face as looking ashen gray during the episode. She called 911 and by the time she returned to his side approximately 30 seconds later, he was already waking up and asking what happened. She states he was fully alert and conversational within one minute of the event. There was no preceding cry, no tonic stiffening, no eye deviation, and no frothing at the mouth. The second episode occurred while seated at the dinner table, and his wife again witnessed brief limb jerking for several seconds. He was referred to neurology for concern of new-onset seizures but the appointment was not for another two weeks. He has also noticed intermittent lightheadedness and a sensation of his heart 'pausing' or 'skipping' over the past two months, particularly when climbing stairs. He denies chest pain, sustained palpitations, shortness of breath at rest, or exertional dyspnea beyond his baseline. He denies any prior seizure history, head trauma, or family history of epilepsy. He has no history of aura, tongue biting, prolonged confusion, or prolonged shaking episodes.
